---
title: "Package release"
description: "Versions the package, tags it and drafts a GitHub release with semantic-release."
---

`package-release.yml` runs [semantic-release](https://semantic-release.gitbook.io)
on `main`. From the [Conventional Commits](commitlint.qmd) since the last
release it

1. works out the next version (`fix:` → patch, `feat:` → minor,
   `feat!:` or a `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer → major) — no release if
   nothing qualifies;
2. writes it to `DESCRIPTION` and commits that as
   `chore(release): set Description file to <version>`;
3. tags the commit with the plain version (`1.2.0`, no `v` prefix);
4. drafts a GitHub release with generated release notes — publish it
   yourself after a final look.

It doesn't comment on or label the issues and pull requests in the release,
and doesn't open an issue when a release fails — the failure shows in the
Actions tab.

It is normally started by the [release chain](release.qmd), not directly.

## Configuration

If your repository has a `.releaserc.json` in its root, it is used as is.
Otherwise the shared configuration of this repository is used, from the
same version of the workflows you call (`@main`, a tag, …).

The shared configuration reads commits with the `conventionalcommits`
preset, so a `!` after the type (`feat!:`) makes a major release as well
as a `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer does. semantic-release's default preset
(`angular`) only knows the footer: a configuration of your own needs
`"preset": "conventionalcommits"` for the commit analyzer and the release
notes generator to behave the same. The preset is installed by the
workflow.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Squash merges
A squash merge leaves one commit, and only its title decides the type
(`feat:`, `fix:`, …) — the commits inside the pull request count only as
its message body. Give the squash commit a conventional title, and keep
a `BREAKING CHANGE:` line in its message if the release should be a
major one.
:::

Only `desc` is installed for R. If your own configuration runs R code that
needs more packages, the release will fail on the missing package.

## Dry run

With `dry-run: true`, semantic-release checks its access, works out the
next version and prints the release notes — but prepares, commits, tags and
publishes nothing. Useful for testing the chain on a real repository.
